items.title: A game engine with limits and a hedge
items.prose: Extend level 2's scripted engine. Trades now fill only up to your room under the limit. A hedge contract pays the first card's value; at a `hedge` event you trade it to hold minus your position. The tests run three seeded scripts from `make_script` and some edge cases.

widget.solution:
def full_game(script, rule, limit=3, n_cards=3):
    """Run a scripted card game with a position limit and
    a hedge contract that pays the first card's value.
    Events, in order:
      ("reveal", v)  a card of value v turns over
      ("buy", k)     the interviewer buys k at your ask
      ("sell", k)    the interviewer sells k at your bid
      ("hedge", p)   trade the hedge contract at price p
                     so you hold minus your position in it
    A trade fills only up to your room: limit + position
    to sell, limit - position to buy.
    rule(fair, position) gives (bid, ask); use
    card_sum_fair(revealed, n_cards) for the fair value.
    Return (pnl, max_position): pnl is cash plus position
    times the true sum plus the hedge times the first
    card, a Fraction; max_position is the largest
    absolute position held."""
    revealed, pos, hedge = [], 0, 0
    cash, peak = Fraction(0), 0
    for kind, x in script:
        if kind == "reveal":
            revealed.append(x)
            continue
        if kind == "hedge":
            trade = -pos - hedge
            cash -= trade * x
            hedge += trade
            continue
        bid, ask = rule(card_sum_fair(revealed, n_cards), pos)
        if kind == "buy":
            k = min(x, limit + pos)
            pos -= k
            cash += k * ask
        else:
            k = min(x, limit - pos)
            pos += k
            cash -= k * bid
        peak = max(peak, abs(pos))
    first = revealed[0] if revealed else 0
    return cash + pos * sum(revealed) + hedge * first, peak

items.title: Before every quote
items.prose: A risk routine runs before each quote in a game with a limit, a bankroll and a hedge.
items.question: Put the checks in order, and leave out the one that does not belong.

lines.text: Check your position against the limit: what room is left each side?
Check the bankroll against the stake: can you bear the worst case?
Check whether a hedge is available, and what crossing its spread costs.
Raise the size when you feel sure of the value.
lines.why: Size by risk, not by conviction. A strong feeling does not change the limit or the bankroll.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The quote comes last, after every risk check.

byKey.conv: Size by risk, not by conviction. A strong feeling does not change the limit or the bankroll.
byKey.left-out: Each risk check belongs; only the size-by-feeling line goes.

explain.text: The limit says how much you may trade, and the bankroll how much you can lose. The hedge says what risk you can remove, and only then is the quote safe. Conviction sets none of these.

items.title: A full game, narrated
items.prompt:
Replay lesson 13's game aloud, as if to an interviewer. Three cards come from one deck: 4, 6 and 5. Use width 4, limit 3 and a skew of 0.5 a lot. The interviewer buys 1 at your ask on turn 1 and tries to sell at 19 after the 4. Then they buy at 20.5 on turn 4 and sell at 16 after the 6.

Take about ten minutes, kept with a watch. Say every fair value with its arithmetic and every quote with its reason. Say your position and P&L after every trade and card. There is no recording: write it out afterwards, then mark it.
items.model:
**Before the game (30 seconds).** "Three cards from one deck. Each averages $364/52 = 7$, so fair is 21. My width is 4 while three cards are unseen, my limit is 3, and I skew 0.5 a lot. I quote 19 at 23 for 1."

**Turn 1: they buy at 23.** "Short 1 at 23, up £2 at fair 21. A buyer may know something, and I am short, so I move up 0.5: 19.5 at 23.5."

**Card 1, a 4.** "The deck holds 360 in 51 cards. Fair is $4 + 2 \times 360/51 = 308/17$, about 18.12. Short 1 at 23, I am up £4.88. Centre $18.12 + 0.5 = 18.62$, call it 18.5: 16.5 at 20.5." They try to sell at 19 and miss my 16.5 bid: updating saved me from a seller who knew.

**Turn 4: they buy at 20.5.** "Short 2 now, cash £43.50, up £7.26 at 18.12. One more lot and I am at the limit. Centre 19.12, call it 19: 17 at 21."

**Card 2, a 6.** "The 50 cards left hold 354. Fair is $10 + 354/50 = 17.08$. Short 2, I am up £9.34. Centre 18.08: 16 at 20."

**Turn 6: they sell at 16.** "I buy 1 back. Short 1, cash £27.50, up £10.42 at 17.08. Centre 17.58, call it 17.5: 15.5 at 19.5."

**Settlement.** The last card is a 5, the sum 15. "Short 1 against cash £27.50: +£12.50. My trades made 8, 5.50 and −1 against 15. The −1 was an inventory trade that halved my risk."

**Review.** "With a king the same quotes make £4.50, so I grade the quotes, not the P&L. The limit was never reached, and every number had its reason."

rubric.text: States each fair value with its arithmetic: 21, 308/17 (18.12) and 427/25 (17.08).
Gives each quote with its width and skew: 19/23, 19.5/23.5, 16.5/20.5, 17/21, 16/20, 15.5/19.5.
Says the position and P&L at fair after every trade and card: +2, +4.88, +7.26, +9.34, +10.42, then +12.50.
Names the turn 3 miss as adverse selection avoided by updating.
Watches the limit: notes short 2 is one lot from 3.
Reviews by quotes, not by P&L: gives the king case, +£4.50.
Speaks with no silent working and no unexplained change of fair value.

items.title: Mock round, part 2: say it
items.prompt:
Narrate the mock round you just played, aloud and timed: about ten minutes. Use the model run's quotes and trades, or your own. Before the first quote the interviewer also offers a side bet. It pays evens on a coin that lands your way with chance 0.6, and you have £100. Choose and justify your stake.

Say each fair value with its arithmetic and each width with its reason. Cover each trade, the limit and the bet size. End with the final P&L and a short review. Then write it out and mark it.
items.model:
**Before any card.** "Each card averages 7, so fair is 21. Three unseen cards, so width 4: 19 at 23 for 1. Limit 3, skew 0.5 a lot."

**Side bet.** "You offer evens on a coin that lands my way with chance 0.6, from a £100 bankroll. Kelly is $0.6 - 0.4 = 0.2$, so I stake £20, not £100: the expected gain is £4, and one loss cannot end me."

**Turn 1: they sell at 19.** "Long 1 at 19, up £2 at 21. A seller may know something, and I am long, so I move down: 18.5 at 22.5."

**Card 1, an 8.** "The deck holds 356 in 51. Fair is $8 + 2 \times 356/51 = 1120/51$, about 21.96. Long 1, up £2.96. Centre $21.96 - 0.5 = 21.46$, call it 21.5: 19.5 at 23.5." They try to buy at 23 and miss my 23.5 ask.

**Turn 5: they sell at 19.5.** "Long 2, cash −£38.50, up £5.42 at 21.96. One more lot reaches the limit, so my next centre drops by another 0.5."

**Card 2, a jack.** "19 shown; 345 in 50 cards. Fair is $19 + 345/50 = 25.9$. Long 2, up £13.30. Centre 24.9, call it 25: 23 at 27."

**Turn 7: they buy at 27.** "I sell 1 at 27, so I am long 1, cash −£11.50, up £14.40 at 25.9. Centre 25.4, call it 25.5: 23.5 at 27.5."

**Settlement.** The last card is a jack: the sum is 30. "Long 1 against cash −£11.50: +£18.50. Edges +11, +10.50 and −3 against 30. The −3 sale cut my long to 1 before the last card."

**Review.** "The stale 19 at 23 would have sold twice at 23 to someone who had seen high cards: −£3. Updating without the skew makes £21 with twice the position. I grade the quotes and the risk, and the bet size followed Kelly."

rubric.text: Fair values with arithmetic: 21, then 1120/51 (21.96), then 259/10 (25.9).
Widths with reasons: 4 while cards are unseen.
Responds to each trade: moves down after a sale to them, up after a buy, with information and inventory named.
Respects the limit: notes long 2 is one lot from 3.
Sizes the side bet by Kelly: £20 of £100, with the reason that a full stake can be ruined.
States the final P&L, +£18.50 for the model run, and reviews the quotes, not only the result.
Spoken clearly, with no silent working.

items.title: A coin and dice market, aloud
items.question: Start the clock and play the round aloud. Then mark your answer against the model.

widget.prompt:
The interviewer says: "I flip a coin you cannot see. Heads, I roll two dice; tails, I roll four. The contract pays the total of the dice I roll. Make me a market, good for 2 lots." Skew 0.5 a lot and choose your own widths.

The round then runs in this order. Answer each step aloud before you read the next.

1. They buy 1 at your ask.
2. They show the first die: a 6.
3. They sell you 2 at your bid.
4. They show the coin: heads.
5. They buy 1 at your ask.
6. They show the last die: a 2.

Say every quote as you make it, with its fair value, why it is that wide and why it moved. Say your position and P&L at fair after each trade. Then answer the follow-ups.
followUps: I had seen the coin before every trade. How wide should your opening quote have been?
Why did your width barely shrink after the 6?
You made edge on every trade and still made nothing. Was it a good round?
widget.model:
**Opening quote.** "Heads means two dice, which average 7. Tails means four, which average 14. Each happens half the time, so fair is $\tfrac12 \times 7 + \tfrac12 \times 14 = 10.5$. The total lands near 7 or near 14, rarely near 10.5, so a tight quote is a bet on the coin. I go 5 wide: 8 at 13, for 2 lots."

**1. They buy 1 at 13.** "I sell 1 at 13 against fair 10.5: £2.50 of edge, so I am up £2.50. A buyer may have seen the coin, and I am short, so I move up 0.5. Centre 11: 8.5 at 13.5."

**2. The first die is a 6.** "The 6 takes the place of a die worth 3.5. Heads leaves one die to come, worth 3.5; tails leaves three, worth 10.5. Fair is $6 + \tfrac12 \times 3.5 + \tfrac12 \times 10.5 = 13$. I sold at 13, so my P&L at fair is £0. The coin still swings the rest by 3.5 either way, so I narrow only to 4 wide. Short 1 puts my centre at 13.5: 11.5 at 15.5."

**3. They sell 2 at 11.5.** "I buy 2, so I am long 1. Each lot has £1.50 of edge, £3 in all. My cash is $13 - 23 = -10$, so at fair 13 I am up £3. A seller of 2 may know the coin is heads, and I am long, so I move down. Centre 12.5: 10.5 at 14.5."

**4. The coin is heads.** "Two dice, and the 6 is one of them, so fair is $6 + 3.5 = 9.5$. Long 1 with cash −£10, I am down £0.50. Only one die is left, so I tighten to 2 wide. Long 1 puts my centre at 9: 8 at 10."

**5. They buy 1 at 10.** "I sell 1 and I am flat, with £0.50 of edge. My cash is $-10 + 10 = 0$, so my P&L is £0 whatever the last die shows."

**6. The last die is a 2.** "The total is 8 and I hold nothing, so I end on £0."

**Review.** "The three trades made £6 of edge against fair at the time: $2.5 + 3 + 0.5 = 6$. Inventory gave it back: I was short 1 while fair rose 2.5, then long 1 while it fell 3.5. The quotes were sound; the cost was holding a lot through the coin."

**Why these widths.** I quote about half an sd each side, to the nearest 0.5. One die has variance $35/12$, so two dice have $35/6$ and four have $35/3$. A case's $E[X^2]$ is its variance plus its mean squared: $35/6 + 49$ for heads and $35/3 + 196$ for tails. Their average is 131.25, so the variance is $131.25 - 10.5^2 = 21$: an sd of 4.58 and a half-width of 2.5. After the 6, the same steps for the dice still to come, one or three, give $67.08 - 7^2 = 18.08$: an sd of 4.25 and a half-width of 2. After heads one die is left: an sd of 1.71 and a half-width of 1.

**The follow-ups.** (1) Whoever sees the coin values the total at 7 on heads and sells at my 8 bid. On tails they value it at 14 and buy at my 13 ask. Either way they take £1 a lot. Only 7 at 14 or wider stops it: a half-width of 3.5, the coin's own swing. (2) The 6 removed one die's spread, but the hidden coin still swung the rest by 3.5 either way. So the sd fell only from 4.58 to 4.25. Showing the coin took it to 1.71, a single die. (3) Yes, judged by the quotes: every trade was at a better price than fair at the time, £6 in all. Fair then moved against each position and took the £6 back. One change: after the sale of 2, with the coin still hidden, I would quote 1 lot until the coin shows.

rubric.text: A quote with its fair value. Tick only if you said each quote as you made it, with its fair value, centred at fair minus 0.5 times your position. With the model's widths they are 8 at 13, 8.5 at 13.5, 11.5 at 15.5, 10.5 at 14.5 and 8 at 10.

The update after information. Tick only if all three fair values come with their arithmetic. 10.5 is half of 7 plus half of 14. 13 after the 6 is $6 + \tfrac12 \times 3.5 + \tfrac12 \times 10.5$, and 9.5 after heads is $6 + 3.5$. A new quote follows each reveal.

The reasons for width and skew. Tick only if both are said. The width is wide while the coin is hidden, since the total lands near 7 or near 14. It narrows little after the 6 and drops to one die's spread after heads. Each move after a trade names information and inventory: up after the buy, down after the sale.
Position and P&L at fair after each step (model figures): +£2.50, £0, +£3, −£0.50, then £0. The review says £6 of edge went back on inventory.
Follow-up 1: against someone who sees the coin, the quote must reach 7 at 14, a half-width of 3.5.

feedback.generic: Compare what you said with the model and tick the rubric.

explain.text: Fair moves from 10.5 to 13 after the 6 and to 9.5 after heads, each said with its arithmetic. The width stays wide until the coin shows, because the coin alone swings the total 3.5 either way. The quotes earned £6 of edge and inventory gave it back, so judge the quotes, not the £0.
